documents.abstract: Remote Utilization Management has emerged as an alternative nursing role for Filipino United States Registered Nurses, yet evidence concerning their working conditions and efficiency remains limited. This study examined the relationship between work environment factors and work efficiency and developed an evidence-based training program. Methods: A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was used among 158 Filipino USRNs working in remote Utilization Management. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring physical work environment, technological support, workload, organizational support, communication, work-life balance, leadership, productivity, accuracy, timeliness, decision making, and job performance. Frequency, percentage, mean, independent samples t test, analysis of variance, Welch’s analysis, and Pearson correlation were employed. Results: Respondents generally reported high levels of work environment and work efficiency. Physical work environment and technological support were the strongest workplace dimensions, while workload and work-life balance were comparatively lowest. Quality and accuracy emerged as the strongest efficiency dimension, whereas productivity was comparatively lowest. Work environment and efficiency differed significantly according to educational attainment, civil status, nursing experience, and remote Utilization Management experience, but not according to age or sex. All work environment dimensions had very strong positive relationships with productivity, accuracy, timeliness, decision making, and overall performance. Discussion: The findings indicate that favorable physical, technological, organizational, relational, and psychosocial conditions are integral to efficient remote nursing practice. The REMOTE-UM EXCEL Program was proposed to strengthen ergonomics, technology competence, workflow management, communication, evidence based decisions, leadership, psychological safety, and work-life boundaries. Organizations should implement integrated workplace interventions and evaluate their effects through longitudinal and performance-based measures to support sustained quality, employee well-being, and organizational effectiveness.

Healthcare workers are exposed to workplace violence, yet the extent and nature of this exposure may differ considerably across professional groups. Psychosocial working conditions, including high work demands, emotional demands, working-time pressures and employment relations, may shape the conditions in which workplace violence occurs and is experienced. This study investigates psychosocial risks, workplace violence and symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress among nurses, physicians, healthcare assistants and administrative staff, and examines whether workplace violence is statistically associated with the relationship between psychosocial risks and these symptoms. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 289 Portuguese healthcare workers using three validated instruments: the Psychosocial Risk Factors Scale (INSAT_ERPS), the Aggression and Violence at Work Scale and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21). Group differences were tested with Kruskal–Wallis tests, associations with Spearman correlations, and mediation and moderation analyses were performed using SPSS and the PROCESS macro. Results showed that workplace violence affected all professional groups but was more intense among nurses. Psychosocial risk was strongly associated with workplace violence, and this association did not differ across professional groups. However, neither psychosocial risks nor violence were associated with depression, anxiety or stress, and no statistically significant indirect association was observed. These findings highlight the importance of addressing workplace violence as an organizational and occupational health issue rather than a problem confined to specific professions.

A written music score specifies what notes should be played, but much of the musical meaning of a performance comes from how those notes are interpreted: pianists shape timing, dynamics, tempo, and articulation to communicate structure, style, and emotion. Modeling this expressive aspect of music matters for music education, digital performance rendering, and creative AI systems, and is difficult precisely because the same score admits many different but musically valid interpretations.In this paper, we present YQX+, a benchmarking framework for probabilistic modeling of expressive piano performance. YQX+ shifts the focus from demonstrating a single rendering system to comparing how different models capture the expressive variation observed in human performance. To make that comparison possible, it fixes the prediction task, a shared multi-scale contextual feature representation, and a common evaluation protocol, so that model families are trained and compared on equal footing. Given a symbolic score, every model in the suite predicts the same note-level expressive parameters, including beat period, velocity, timing deviation, and articulation ratio, from features that capture local note context, harmonic texture, phrase structure, and score markings. The suite takes the original YQX Gaussian mixture model (GMM) as its reference point and extends it to XGBoost, variational autoencoders, and conditional flow-matching models.To support perceptual evaluation, we also introduce PerformanceMOS, a data-driven estimator of perceived expressive quality and performance skill from symbolic piano performances. Experiments show that larger-capacity XGBoost and \((\beta)\)-VAE models achieve lower timing and articulation errors than prior baselines, including DExter and VirtuosoNet, and obtain the highest predicted mean opinion scores (MOS). These findings establish YQX+ as a systematic benchmark for probabilistic modeling of piano performance expression, with PerformanceMOS providing a scalable proxy for human listening evaluation. The code, trained models, and evaluation scripts are available at \texttt{https://github.com/kkwsts/YQX-Plus}.

Computer-based managerial systems are part of the digital infrastructure of work, with potential implications for employee demands and discretion. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, this study examines task allocation, work scheduling and performance monitoring as distinct functions and their parallel indirect associations with engagement and intention to quit through work intensity and autonomy. Weighted least squares mean- and variance-adjusted structural equation models were estimated for 26,504 employees in 35 European countries using the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey. The measures capture reported computer involvement rather than verified artificial intelligence capabilities. Engagement and autonomy were modelled as latent factors, and quit intention as an ordinal outcome. All three practices were positively associated with work intensity. Task allocation was positively associated with autonomy, whereas monitoring was negatively associated with autonomy; scheduling’s negative autonomy association was less robust to contextual fixed effects. Task allocation showed opposing indirect engagement associations through intensity and autonomy, whereas monitoring showed negative associations through both pathways. Intensity-related indirect associations with quit intention were consistently positive, while autonomy-related indirect associations were not statistically significant in the primary or fixed-effects models. Sensitivity analyses supported the main directional patterns, while exploratory country diagnostics indicated incomplete measurement invariance and heterogeneous slopes. The findings inform the evaluation of digital management by distinguishing functions associated with greater demands and greater autonomy from those associated with greater demands and reduced autonomy. The cross-sectional design does not establish causal mediation or uniform cross-country relationships.

Estudo observacional, transversal, descritivo e analítico, com abordagem quantitativa, destinado a analisar a associação entre riscos ergonômicos, estresse ocupacional e queixas musculoesqueléticas em bombeiros militares vinculados ao Comando Geral do Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Estado do Pará, em Belém, Pará, Brasil. Os riscos ergonômicos serão avaliados por meio do Job Factors Questionnaire; o estresse ocupacional, pela versão brasileira resumida da Job Stress Scale; e as queixas musculoesqueléticas, pelo Questionário Nórdico de Sintomas Osteomusculares. O modelo estatístico principal será um modelo linear generalizado misto logístico (GLMM), com intercepto aleatório por participante e observações correspondentes às regiões anatômicas avaliadas. O Plano de Análise Estatística foi consolidado e congelado internamente em 29 de agosto de 2026, antes do início da coleta de dados. A coleta teve início em 31 de agosto de 2026 e permanece em andamento na data deste registro. Nenhuma análise descritiva ou inferencial dos dados do estudo foi realizada antes do registro público. O registro tem como finalidade documentar prospectivamente, em relação ao acesso aos resultados e à realização das análises, as hipóteses, os desfechos, as exposições, o planejamento amostral, os modelos estatísticos e as análises de sensibilidade previamente estabelecidas. Dashboards are central to contemporary organizations aiming to ‘datafy’ decision making and management practices. As one of the primary media through which people engage with digital data in organizational contexts, dashboards shape how data is accessed and perceived. Despite their ubiquity, there is limited understanding of how dashboards mediate data visibility and influence observers’ perceptions of the data. Drawing on theories of mediation and diagrammatics, this paper analyzes the ‘generic form’ shared by all dashboards. It then identifies the modes of observation encouraged by dashboards, revealing how they position their observers. While grounded in theoretical arguments, the analysis incorporates empirical examples from a study on the datafication of Human Resource Management. The paper makes two key contributions. It emphasizes the critical role of visual forms in datafication processes, and it highlights the organizational implications of the use of a specific kind of visual medium: the dashboard.

Shared e-scooters are now common in urban transportation, but safety planning remains limited by a lack of exposure-based, spatially detailed crash risk measures. This study applied an exposure-based approach to identify high-risk e-scooter corridors in Nashville, Tennessee, combining 92 police-reported, motor-vehicle-involved e-scooter crashes with trip-kilometer exposure data over a 45-month period. Crashes were assigned to corridors by rider direction of travel, and rates were calculated per 100,000 vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) citywide and by corridor. Across more than five million e-scooter kilometers of exposure, the citywide crash rate was 1.84 per 100,000 VKT, and 82.6% of crashes occurred at intersections or driveways. The 25 corridors accounted for 75.0% of crashes and 70.9% of VKT, with a combined rate (1.94 per 100,000 VKT) statistically indistinguishable from the rest of Nashville (1.58; p = 0.34). Corridor-level rates were nonetheless heterogeneous (chi-square = 96.17, df = 24, p < 0.001), with unadjusted rates ranging from 0.69 to 24.49 crashes per 100,000 VKT; empirical Bayes shrinkage reduced this spread to roughly 3.7-fold. Three corridors, Shelby Avenue, 21st Avenue, and West End Avenue, exceeded the citywide rate individually, with the first two remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Exposure-adjusted corridor rates gave a different picture of risk than crash counts alone: citywide averages concealed substantial street-level variation, supporting corridor-level exposure measures as a screening tool for micromobility safety, though individual designations remain exploratory rather than confirmatory. These results let agencies combine trip and crash data to target safety investment at high-risk corridors.

Elite strength and conditioning (S&C) coaches occupy a critical but underexamined position as first-line users of sports-science technology, responsible for translating raw athlete-monitoring data into immediate training decisions. Through seven semi-structured interviews with elite S & C coaches across NCAA Division I, professional, and Olympic contexts, we identify four recurring breakdowns in their daily data work: fragmented vendor ecosystems, metric overload, scale and staffing constraints and staff turnover. Static mockup elicitation during interviews revealed a consistent preference for simple, interpretable interfaces that foreground selected metrics and concise explanations over dense data displays. We position elite S&C coaches as a distinct user group whose needs are poorly served by current systems, and propose four design priorities: integration stability, selective metrics with contextual explanation, scale-aware views, and governance continuity, to guide future coach-facing sports-science interface design.

At unsignalized midblock crosswalks (UMCs), visual obstructions created by bike lane buffers can substantially affect drivers’ pedestrian detection and yielding behavior. However, limited evidence is available regarding how different types of bike lane buffers influence driving performance through changes in visual attention and cognitive workload. To address this issue, four representative bike lane buffer scenarios—Lawn, Railing, Bush, and Tree—were developed in a driving simulation environment. Vehicle operation parameters and eye-tracking data were collected simultaneously to investigate drivers’ behavioral and visual responses while approaching a crosswalk. The results showed that highly obstructive buffers significantly delayed pedestrian detection and weakened drivers’ early risk perception. In the Bush and Tree scenarios, pedestrians were detected at distances of only about 18 m from the crosswalk, representing a reduction of more than 40% compared with the low-obstruction conditions. As a consequence, drivers exhibited lower terminal braking speeds, higher maximum deceleration rates, and more abrupt braking maneuvers. The mean braking initiation distance in the Bush and Tree scenarios was approximately 48 m, which was more than 10 m shorter than that observed under the Lawn and Railing conditions. Eye-tracking analyses further revealed that highly obstructive environments significantly increased fixation duration on roadside areas while reducing the effective visual search range. In addition, the proportions of saccades and blinks decreased to approximately 3%, whereas the coefficient of variation of pupil diameter increased to 0.23, indicating elevated cognitive workload and mental stress. These findings demonstrate that visual obstructions associated with bike lane buffers can adversely affect drivers’ hazard perception, visual search behavior, and braking responses. The study provides empirical evidence to support the safety evaluation and design optimization of bike lane buffers near unsignalized midblock crosswalks.

Designing Knowledge Management Systems (KMSs) for higher education requires addressing complex human–technology interactions, especially where staff turnover and changing roles create challenges for reusing knowledge. While advances in process mining and Generative AI enable new ways of designing features to support knowledge management, existing KMSs often overlook the realities of educators' workflows, leading to low adoption and limited impact. This paper presents findings from a two-year human-centred design study with 108 higher education teachers, examining iterative co-design and evaluation of GoldMind – a KMS supporting in-the-flow knowledge management during digital teaching tasks. Through three design–evaluation cycles, we examined teachers' task-evaluations and how feedback informed refinements. Insights are synthesised across three themes: (1) Technology Lessons from user interaction data, (2) Design Considerations shaped by co-design and usability testing, and (3) Human Factors, including cognitive load and knowledge behaviours, analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (in the last iteration). This study demonstrates that embedding human-centred, workflow-integrated KMSs can improve task efficiency, reduce cognitive load, and support knowledge reuse, while shaping educators' knowledge management behaviours through context-aware and proactive support. However, findings are based on a single-institution, controlled evaluation, limiting generalisability and requiring longitudinal, in-the-wild studies to assess adoption and impact.

Project-based learning (PjBL) is common in computing education, but traditional assessments of PjBL often fail to capture higher-order thinking (HOT), especially in transfer contexts. This study introduces ''design problems'' (DPs): concise, scenario-based prompts that require applying project concepts in new situations, to address this gap. We examined instructor perceptions, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate DPs, and student experiences. Surveys of 31 instructors, evaluation of 80 LLM-generated DPs, and student performance data showed that while instructors value DPs, creation effort is a barrier. LLMs helped by producing high-quality prompts with strong expert agreement. Students rated DPs from different LLMs similarly, and their performance on DP tasks showed negligible correlation with traditional project grades, suggesting DPs may capture distinct aspects of HOT. Keystroke data also suggested deeper cognitive engagement of students through planning and revision behaviors. Overall, DPs appear to be a useful complement to traditional assessments, especially in situations where AI use or collaboration may undermine individual learning.

Purpose : N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) is a polar aprotic solvent that is extensively used in the production of synthetic leather, polyurethane products, resins, adhesives and surface coatings. Potential sources of occupational exposures are mixing, formulation, coating, solvent transfer, cleaning, maintenance, and spill-response. DMF may be inhaled and absorbed through intact skin, which means that total internal dose for a particular worker may be underestimated by only measuring DMF in the air. Liver is a known target organ of DMF toxicity, and reports of increased liver enzymes and, less frequently, clinically significant liver injury have been reported in workers occupationally exposed to DMF. Increases in liver-function tests, however, are non-specific and can occur in people who drink too much alcohol and/or are obese, and/or may be caused by metabolic disease associated with steatotic liver disease, viral hepatitis, certain medicines (prescribed or not) or other exposures that may occur at work. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation of possible liver damage from DMF should include exposure history, workplace monitoring, biological monitoring, repeated clinical evaluations, and the careful consideration of other causes of liver damage. Objective : The aim of this study is to find the relationship between DMF exposure and liver injury in the workers working in the synthetic leather, polyurethane, resin and surface-coating industries. It will consider exposure by inhalation and skin contact, estimate internal exposure as measured by urinary markers, review liver-function patterns as they change over time, determine if another source of liver injury or exposure may have occurred, and determine if a failure of workplace controls or medical surveillance could have led to exposure. The results will help to inform evidence-based occupational-health and medico-legal decisions about the possibility and level of occupational contribution to liver disease. Methods : An occupational-health study using a mixed-methods approach will be conducted with workers who may be at risk for DMF, such as mixers, formulators, coating operators, solvent-transfer workers, cleaners, maintenance workers, and waste-handling workers. A standardised occupational history will document job titles, length of employment, work patterns, frequency of tasks, use of DMF containing products, past chemical exposures, spillages, symptoms, hygiene practices and use and suitability of personal protective equipment (PPE). Task specific workplace exposure assessments will be carried out and personal air sampling will be used, wherever possible, especially during transfer, mixing, coating, cleaning and maintenance activities. The results of the air-monitoring will be evaluated against relevant occupational exposure concentrations with an understanding that an exposure below the airborne concentration limit does not mean there is no significant dermal absorption. The dermal exposure potential will be evaluated by conducting facility observations and interviews with workers, which will include direct hands-on contact with the material, use of contaminated gloves and clothing, gloves used, gloves replaced, local exhaust ventilation, housekeeping, spill control, washing facility, training, and working practices. The urinary concentrations of N-methylformamide (NMF) and N-acetyl-S-(N-methylcarbamoyl)cysteine (AMCC) will be measured for internal DMF exposure. These are markers of systemic exposure from all routes of exposure including inhalation and skin contact. Ideally, urine samples will be collected at the end of shift and end of work week, or at other suitable times depending on the toxicokinetic properties of the biomarker. Urine dilutions, e.g. creatinine, specific gravity etc., will be corrected and results interpreted taking into account the timing of the sample, the analytical procedure and available biological guidance values. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels, bilirubin, albumin and international normalised ratio (INR) will be measured at regular intervals. These tests will assist in the identification of hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed liver injury patterns and be useful in identifying transient, persistent or progressive liver injuries. Symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, pruritus and constitutional symptoms will also be recorded. Systematic assessment of potential confounding factors and alternative diagnosis. Alcohol intake, BMI, presence of diabetes, metabolic disease, pre-existing liver disease, other hepatotoxic chemicals and drug or supplement use will be recorded. Investigations may consist of a hepatology specialist review, abdominal ultrasound and hepatitis B and C testing, where clinically appropriate and consented to. There will be a structured medico-legal review, combining evidence from 4 domains – exposure, biological plausibility, individual clinical disease and duty of care. Occupational history and occupational monitoring will support the results of urinary biomarkers as evidence of internal exposure. The adequacy of engineering controls, local exhaust ventilation, training, spill management, hazard communication and medical surveillance will be taken into account in the duty of care assessment. Challenging with the drug after a possible hepatotoxic reaction will not take place. Expected Results : The study will not pre-judge causation as there is currently no data. It is anticipated to see if the workers with high overall or task specific exposure would have higher levels of urinary NMF and AMCC, and if these workers would have more frequent and persistent liver-test abnormalities. It will also be evaluated if liver enzymes improve if DMF exposure is reduced or eliminated, if follow up is available. Importantly, the analysis will differentiate isolated elevations of enzymes from a pattern of occupationally related disease. Conclusions :Concurring inhalational and dermal exposure to DMF is an occupational-health hazard that can be prevented. Task-based exposure assessment, urinary biomarkers, serial liver tests, clinical differential diagnosis and structured medico-legal analysis is a better approach for assessing possible occupational hepatotoxicity than liver enzymes alone. Decisions regarding the possibility, probability and highly probable occupational contribution will be based on the overall evidence and distinct from legal liability.PPE, training, spillage or medical surveillance had a significant impact on the workers.

documents.abstract: Near-miss events in the workplace serve as important signals for occupational accident prevention, and organizational responses to near-miss reports may influence employees’ perceived organizational support (POS). the association between organizational response patterns to near-miss reports and POS has not been sufficiently examined. This longitudinal study used data from an online cohort study of Japanese workers conducted at baseline (March 2023) and follow-up (December 2023). The analysis included 1,168 non-managerial workers who had experienced at least one near-miss event. Participants were categorized into four groups based on reporting behavior and the adequacy of organizational responses: reporting with adequate response, reporting with partial response, reporting with no response (reference), and no reporting. Associations between response patterns and POS at follow-up were examined using linear regression analysis. Employees in the reporting with adequate response (B = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.71–3.61) and reporting with partial response (B = 1.68, 95% CI: 0.12–3.23) groups showed significantly higher POS at follow-up compared with the reporting with no response group. The no reporting group also showed significantly higher POS (B = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.13–3.12). No significant moderating effect of company size was observed. These findings suggest that the quality of organizational responses to near-miss reports is associated with POS regardless of company size. Employees who reported near-miss events but received no organizational response showed the lowest POS, even lower than those who did not report. These findings highlight the importance of adequate follow-up and communication after near-miss reporting.

documents.abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.

Background Ergonomics is an often-overlooked component of operative education. Early intervention can protect residents from physical stress and long-term musculoskeletal injury. Our aim is to evaluate residents during a simulated suturing exercise and assess the impact of self-evaluation on ergonomics. Methods Following informed consent, surgical residents performed a simulated complex wound closure, blinded to the study’s focus. Following initial closure, residents reviewed their videos with an ergonomic self-assessment guide, repeated the exercise, and completed a post-survey. Representative video clips were analyzed to measure elbow, spine, and neck angles. Standard angles were defined as 90–110° for elbow, < 10° for spine, and < 25° for neck. Results Twenty residents participated across four post-graduate years (PGY): five PGY-4, four PGY-3, four PGY-2, and seven PGY-1. Across all participants, we found significant reduction in spine (12.5° vs 5.1°, p = 0.016) and neck (58.5° vs 46.4°, p = 0.004) angle during the second exercise, but no difference in elbow angle (102.7° vs 101.7°, p = 0.744). The post-survey revealed most residents think about their ergonomics in the operating room at least weekly (75%) and feel physical strain (95%). All residents (100%) reported improved awareness of ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. Discussion Our study demonstrated a resident self-assessment of ergonomics led to significant improvement in spinal and neck angles in a simulated exercise with increased awareness of operative ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. These findings support integration of ergonomic education early in surgical training to help reduce physical strain and promote operative longevity.

In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

Avoiding loss-of-control events will be key to industry and society as AI technology is employed in various critical processes. In this article, we assess a hypothetical instability situation of an AGI − a singularity event − from a safety science standpoint. We present one way to describe the process of how a real time Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in its interaction with the environment may set it in a runaway condition. Our goal is clarifying general and structural control issues of strong real time AI for design, safeguarding and legislation. In cybernetics, instability and hence, the risk of loss-of-control, is a core trait of all highly adaptive systems. Such adaptive behavior can manifest as radical reframing – a pivotal process of a system that enables it to solve very hard challenges, and which requires it to redefine its core concepts, goals, values, plans and procedures. What emerges is the AGI power dilemma ; a double-bind between performance and controllability of a real time system. We discuss the consequences for human control of AGI and prospects for safeguarding when optimizing for power and speed. Moreover, we conclude that the human in the loop approach gives an illusion of safety when the AI is optimized for power.

documents.abstract: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.

Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

This repository provides materials from a professional development programme at Universidad Tecnológica Israel, Ecuador, on designing instruction around authentic professional tasks using the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) model. The programme helps university teachers connect syllabus learning outcomes with the integrated knowledge, skills and attitudes required for professional performance. The materials combine explanatory guides, worked design examples, classroom modelling, participant assignments and design worksheets. A continuing example (i.e., conducting a critical literature review to substantiate the preliminary definition of an educational research problem) illustrates how the design decisions connect across sessions. Participants apply the same principles to tasks from their own disciplines. The materials are shared to document the training and support scholarly discussion, reuse and adaptation in higher education. They describe the programme’s instructional rationale and activities; they do not report an empirical evaluation of its effectiveness.

As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

The rapid digitalisation of financial services has increased individuals’ exposure to online fraud. However, recent literature highlights that identifying a clear profile of fraud victims remains challenging, as individual-level factors examined so far do not fully explain fraud vulnerability. This study examines how financial literacy, digital financial literacy, and financial graph literacy are associated with individuals’ susceptibility to fraud. Moving beyond aggregate measures, the study adopts a multidimensional framework that distinguishes, for both financial and digital financial literacy, between knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, and introduces financial graph literacy as a key capability for interpreting visually presented financial information. The study combines survey-based measures with an embedded experimental task and employs regression and mediation analyses. The findings show that financial and digital financial knowledge are not consistently associated with lower fraud victimization. Higher financial and digital financial attitude scores are associated with lower fraud victimization, whereas higher scores on the financial behavior index are associated with greater reported victimization. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower fraud victimization. Indirect-effect estimates are consistent with partial mediation through overconfidence for digital financial attitude and financial graph literacy. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower end-anchoring, i.e. a disproportionate reliance on the final movement of a stock-price graph, but end-anchoring is not associated with fraud victimization. Overall, the study advances a process-oriented and behaviorally grounded understanding of fraud vulnerability, emphasizing the interplay among literacy components and cognitive biases.

Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

Background: Ensuring a sustainable nursing workforce requires both academic capacity building and a deeper understanding of the experiences that nurture students’ commitment to the profession. In India, rapid growth in nursing education has intersected with changing societal perceptions and competitive career landscapes. This study sought to explore career choice motivations, professional perceptions, and future career intentions among Indian nursing students. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach was gently conducted between April 2025 and June 2026. Phase I involved an online cross-sectional survey (N=1544) across multiple geographical zones. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Group comparison tests, and multiple linear regression modelling were also used. Phase II comprised semi-structured qualitative interviews (N=27) analyzed using Colaizzi’s descriptive phenomenological approach to better contextualize the statistical findings. Quantitative and qualitative strands were integrated via joint display and narrative synthesis. Results: A notable proportion of participants (69.8%) reported considering alternative career choices, most commonly medicine (37.4%) and technical fields (25.8%). Mean domain scores indicated high intrinsic motivation (19.94 ± 4.61) and economic expectations (20.00 ± 4.11), alongside academic stress (20.03 ± 3.90). Multiple regression analysis (F = 5.085, p < 0.001, R² = 0.103) showed that female gender (B = 4.717, p < 0.001) and salary expectations (B = 1.493, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perception scores, whereas career change intention (B = −4.659, p < 0.001) and higher secondary examination marks (B = −1.905, p = 0.002) were negatively associated. Qualitative findings, organized into seven themes and 27 subthemes, provided explanatory context. Students described how entrance exam setbacks, heavy assignment loads, inconsistent mentorship, and social stigma contributed to uncertainty. In contrast, rewarding patient encounters and the development of clinical confidence fostered a growing sense of professional commitment. Conclusion: Indian nursing students navigate diverse pathways into the profession, balancing altruistic goals with practical challenges and evolving career preferences. The results tentatively highlight that supportive career counseling, refined academic requirements, enhanced clinical mentorship, and clear role definitions may help strengthen students' professional identity and support long-term commitment to nursing practice.

Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

Cognitive friction has been described both as productive resistance intended to sustain cognitive engagement and as effort required to overcome obstacles in AI interaction. These uses create uncertainty about the boundaries of the construct and the mechanisms attributed to it across different contexts. To clarify how cognitive friction is defined and distinguished from related constructs, and to map the mechanisms described as generating it across educational, professional, and everyday human–AI interactions. English-language empirical and non-empirical sources will be eligible where they provide substantive conceptual or mechanistic content relevant to cognitive friction or potentially related constructs in human–AI interaction. Eligible evidence may include journal articles, conference papers, theses, substantive commentaries, and full preprints or working papers. Electronic searches were conducted on 22 October 2026 in Scopus, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, arXiv and SSRN. Backward and forward citation searching will supplement these searches. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full texts against predefined eligibility criteria. Two reviewers will independently chart data using a structured Google Sheets workbook. Data will be analysed through descriptive mapping and basic qualitative content analysis. No formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment will be conducted.

The growing integration of cyber, physical, and operational security functions has created a need for assessment approaches that evaluate security convergence as an organisational capability rather than as a set of isolated controls. This article proposes the Converged Security Maturity Index (CSMI), a conceptual maturity model designed to assess the level of integration among cybersecurity, physical security, and operational security within organisations. The model is developed using a design science research approach grounded in a structured review of converged security literature, cyber–physical system security, and existing maturity frameworks. CSMI comprises five progressive maturity levels—Fragmented, Coordinated, Integrated, Unified, and Optimised—and evaluates organisational capabilities across four dimensions: governance and strategy, processes and incident management, technology and infrastructure integration, and human factors and organisational culture. The article describes the architecture of the model and the rationale for each maturity level and dimension and outlines how the framework could be applied in practice through a structured questionnaire in future work. The proposed framework aims to support organisational self-assessment, benchmarking, and identification of convergence gaps across different sectors.

Understanding cognitive biases in cyber attacker behavior can help develop countermeasures that leverage predictable mental shortcuts. This paper analyzes the impact of one such bias, the default effect, on cyber attack decisions. Three forms of this effect are examined: explicit default, association effect, and position effect. The experiment included 85 participants who displayed cybersecurity knowledge based on a screening assessment. The participants performed established behavioral tasks and cyber-adapted scenarios involving host selection, port selection, and password spraying. Our findings confirmed that explicit defaults behave as expected from prior research: people preferred the default option more often under opt-out than opt-in framing. For cyber tasks, the association effect was always present and influential as participants preferred options semantically related to the contextual cues provided. In contrast, position effects failed to emerge when semantically meaningful cues were available. Results offer actionable insights for designing cyber defense systems that leverage predictable attacker heuristics.

To safely and efficiently manage increasing drone traffic, Uncrewed Air Traffic Management (UTM) is currently being developed with high levels of automation. In low-altitude airspace around airports, human supervision remains essential to ensure safe separation between drones and crewed aircraft, requiring transparency to support oversight of automated decision-making. Although transparency has been shown to improve understanding, trust, and performance, relatively little is known about transparency-seeking behavior during real-time supervision. This article presents a novel on-demand interface for tactical UTM, comprising eight information overlays derived from a consolidated transparency taxonomy that unifies previously fragmented transparency constructs. A human-in-the-loop experiment with 16 participants investigated transparency usage under varying traffic conditions, automation failures, and two autonomous path-planning algorithms: the graph-based Zeta*-SIPP and the sampling-based Informed RRT*. The results show that information about the Closest Point of Approach between drones and crewed aircraft was operationally most valuable. During automation failures, participants increasingly requested information about changes in constraints and traffic situations, together with the planner’s internal reasoning, to diagnose failures and guide intervention decisions. Furthermore, the sampling-based planner revealed an important boundary condition for transparency research: the cognitive costs and benefits of algorithmic transparency during real-time supervision depend on the characteristics of the underlying algorithm and how its search process is presented. Overall, this study shows that transparency requirements are dynamic, depending on user needs, operational context, and the underlying autonomy, and that complementary transparency perspectives can be successfully integrated into a single adaptable interface.

Runway overruns rank among the most frequent and economically significant accident categories in commercial aviation, typically arising from the nonlinear combination of performance variabilities during the approach and landing phases. Existing risk models either rely on historical accident databases or treat runway overrun precursors as independent binary events, overlooking the interactive dynamics of everyday flight operations. This paper introduces FRAM-FDM, a quantitative methodology that integrates the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) with Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) to assess and manage operational runway overrun risk from a Safety-II perspective. The methodology deconstructs the approach-and-landing sociotechnical system into functional couplings, quantifies their output variabilities using real flight data recorder (FDR) data, and aggregates them through: (i) linear regression combined with Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) for probabilistic fleet-level risk estimation; (ii) logistic regression with odds-ratio analysis to rank precursor influence; and (iii) metadata-driven scenario simulation in the FRAM Model Visualiser (FMV). Applied to a case study of 110 landings — including one overrun event — from a business jet fleet, the framework identifies airspeed excess at the runway threshold and brake application profile as the dominant risk contributors, demonstrates synergistic risk amplification when multiple variabilities co-occur, and provides actionable guidance for training and procedure reinforcement. FRAM-FDM advances FRAM toward a fully quantitative, data-driven implementation and aligns FDM programmes with Safety-II principles.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used by medical students for academic purposes, yet how patterns of such use relate to academic motivation and self-efficacy remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in the Iranian medical education context. This study examined the frequency and purpose of AI tool use among medical students and their associations with academic motivation and academic self-efficacy. Methods A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among medical students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, in 2026. Using proportionate stratified sampling across four educational stages, 111 students completed a questionnaire package comprising a researcher-developed AI-use instrument (separate frequency and purpose scores), the Persian Academic Motivation Scale, and the Persian College Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Associations between the two AI-use scores and five outcomes (self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, amotivation, and composite positive motivation) were examined using Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction, followed by five multiple linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, educational stage, and GPA. Results Conversational AI tools, most notably ChatGPT, were used by nearly all participants. Both AI-use frequency and purpose were positively correlated with academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, and negatively correlated with amotivation (Spearman ρ = 0.46–0.77; all p < 0.001, surviving Bonferroni correction). In adjusted models, AI-use purpose remained independently associated with all five outcomes (standardized β = 0.32–0.69), whereas AI-use frequency remained independently associated only with self-efficacy (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). GPA was independently associated with intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, but not self-efficacy or amotivation. No significant differences by sex or educational stage were observed. The five models explained 40% to 61% of outcome variance. Conclusions The purpose for which medical students use AI tools showed more consistent independent associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy than frequency of use alone, suggesting that how AI is used may be more relevant to these outcomes than how often it is used. As an observational, cross-sectional study, these findings describe association rather than causal sequence, and contribute context-specific evidence on AI use and its psychological correlates among medical students in Iran.

AI systems err, however, existing Strategies to influence a user’s trust perception can sometimes fail to foster perceptions and assessments that reflect system limitations, with potentially detrimental real-world consequences. In this paper, we introduce a novel Relational Risk (RR) strategy derived from risk communication research to pre-emptively communicate the likelihood of AI error and its potential consequences, foregrounding the costs of AI error, and compare it with existing Strategies (AI accuracy, AI apology). Participants ( ) engaged in an AI-assisted decision-making task with varying Stakes and AI performance, and we measured how these influence perceived AI trustworthiness across relevant perceptual dimensions (transparency, performance, utility). We find that RR enhances perceived AI transparency post-AI errors and encourages healthy scrutiny without diminishing or inflating perceived AI performance or utility. Conversely, AI accuracy boosts perceived AI transparency, performance, and utility under high decision-stakes, increasing system trustworthiness when unwarranted, while apology improves perceived AI utility but does not support system understanding. We contribute an in-depth investigation of how communication strategies shape AI trustworthiness perceptions, reveal important drawbacks of existing approaches, and demonstrate how integrating risk communication theory can enable more appropriate trustworthiness assessments.

documents.abstract: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is progressively transforming emergency abdominal care through high-definition visualization, indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging, robotic-assisted platforms and the emerging integration of artificial intelligence (AI). This narrative review traces the evolution from conventional laparoscopy to fluorescence-guided, robotic-assisted and AI-supported emergency surgery. Publications were identified in PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science, prioritizing guidelines, consensus statements, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and recent clinical studies. Current evidence supports a laparoscopic-first approach in hemodynamically stable patients with acute appendicitis, acute calculous cholecystitis, perforated peptic ulcer and selected cases of adhesive small bowel obstruction, strangulated hernia, complicated diverticulitis and penetrating trauma, whereas open laparotomy remains mandatory in hemorrhagic or septic shock. Near-infrared ICG imaging has expanded from elective to emergency practice for biliary anatomy identification, bowel perfusion assessment and anastomotic decision-making, although prospective emergency data remain limited. Robotic systems offer dexterity, ergonomics and integrated imaging, but emergency use is constrained by availability, cost, docking time and team training. AI is being explored for anatomy recognition, risk prediction, augmented reality and autonomous subtasks, with decision support the most realistic near-term role. The value of these technologies depends less on the technology itself than on patient selection, surgical expertise, team preparedness and institutional readiness.

Online identity typically has been conceptualized either in terms of online social roles or in terms of identification with specific online groups. In this paper we explore whether people can form a meaningful identity from the online domain itself , seeing themselves collectively as ‘online people’, ‘offline people’, or in terms of a hybrid online/offline self-categorization. Results from a survey study of 200 participants supported this idea, such that the means of online, offline, or hybrid person variables were significantly above the midpoint of the scale and the majority of participants identified most strongly in terms of one of these identities. Factor analysis, correlations, variable network analysis, and textual analysis suggested that online and offline social identity are orthogonal constructs. Moreover, online identity was related to, but distinct from, hybrid identity (being a person who lives both online and offline). Supporting predictions derived from social digital identity theory (SDIT), each kind of domain-based identification uniquely predicted higher trust in the relevant ingroup only. Moreover, in line with predictions, online identification uniquely predicted more positive attitudes towards technology. However, contrary to predictions, the different kinds of domain-based social identification did not uniquely predict wellbeing or social cohesion. Hybrid and offline identification also failed to uniquely predict technology attitudes. Furthermore, when controlling for hybrid identification, being more ‘online’ in terms of online technology use did not significantly predict wellbeing or social cohesion outcomes. These findings represent an initial exploration of ‘domain-based’ social identities and their implications.

All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

Recent work in human-computer interaction and allied fields has sought to engage community members as co-designers, facilitators, and decision makers to challenge structural power barriers and knowledge gaps. In this paper, we apply a diverse set of computational techniques to engage and address community concerns surrounding the socio-environmental impacts of the Greenidge Bitcoin mining power plant facility in upstate New York. Through collaborative interactions with community groups, addressing problems ranging from regulatory inertia to thermal water pollution, we aim to facilitate not just the production of new and critical environmental knowledge but also new computationally-supported repertoires of contention: means of contesting the unequal relations of knowledge and power that structure and often determine the outcomes of environmental controversies. We argue such engagements can help support more politically engaged forms of HCI, oriented towards efforts to redress and repair disparities in wealth, knowledge, and influence through strategic sociotechnical interventions and alliances.

Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

Most organisations generate travel and transport and thus influence traffic safety. Nevertheless, their roles and responsibilities for occupational road safety remain poorly understood. This study examines organisational readiness for occupational road safety with a particular focus on the relationship between organisations’ perceptions of traffic safety and the implementation of traffic safety measures. The study is based on a survey of organisational representatives in 109 companies in Sweden in 2025. The survey consists of two questionnaires capturing organisational commitment and reported measures to improve traffic safety in organisations’ roles as employers and transport buyers. An employer questionnaire focuses on traffic safety requirements for employees’ work-related travel and organisational vehicle fleets, while a transport procurement questionnaire captures the requirements on transport procurement. Organisational readiness for occupational road safety is analysed using Organisational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC), including perceived capacity to influence traffic safety, views on responsibility, and the integration of traffic safety into occupational health and safety (OHS) or sustainability practices. The results show that many organisations have policies for work-related travel and set traffic safety requirements for their vehicles, while such requirements in transport procurement remain limited. Regression analyses indicate that organisations with higher readiness are more likely to set traffic safety requirements, particularly regarding work-related travel. The findings highlight the need to strengthen organisations’ awareness of their roles and responsibilities, clarify expectations for organisations from authorities, and further integrate traffic safety into organisational management systems to reduce road traffic fatalities and injuries, in line with the global road safety agenda, often framed as “saving lives beyond 2025”.

documents.abstract: Debates around generative artificial intelligence frequently organise workplace change through automation and augmentation, leaving less visible the organisational work through which human contribution remains interpretable once production is shared with generative systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 women in business-related apprenticeships in England, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and abductive engagement with sociotechnical AI research, labour-process scholarship and feminist accounts of recognition, the study develops a mechanism-oriented account in which organisational rules delimit legitimate AI use, selected execution tasks accelerate, and verification, contextual judgement and accountable decision-making remain attached to apprentices. Where AI-mediated production made polished output a weaker standalone indicator of individual capability, some participants described supplementing performance with additional evidentiary work that rendered contribution, judgement and responsibility more legible to evaluators. This evaluator-facing work is conceptualised as attributional labour, a reconfiguration of pre-existing recognition demands whose form changes when technologically mediated artefacts reveal less about the human competence behind them. The organisational costs and returns associated with this work appeared to vary with occupational hierarchy, managerial proximity and the valuation of administrative and relational work. Augmentation consequently emerges as an organisational recognition settlement in which technical capacity, hidden human work and evaluative authority are redistributed together.

In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

Background. A majority of European countries have heat-health action plans in place or under development, yet the health and social sectors are poorly considered despite their high burden and key role for health system resilience and security. Objectives. This research connects workforce policy and heat-health action policy, aiming to assess preparedness, protection and agency of health and care workers and identify gaps and capacities for implementation. Methods. Qualitative comparative methodology and a country case study design were applied and a rapid assessment of eight European countries performed during August/September 2026. A semi-structed topic guide informed data collection, drawing on policy documents and other secondary sources. Results. No country case study established a dedicated workforce-centred heat-health strategy nor do they have routine workforce-specific heat-health surveillance systems in place. Countries recognise health workers primarily as service providers, rather than as a workforce requiring protection. This approach shapes all areas of heat-health action. Preparedness of health workers shows limited strategic action but with some adaptations at the provider and individual level and in the education sector. Protection remains poorly addressed and equality, gender equality and migrant health workers are largely absent. Professional stakeholders and bottom-up emerging adaptations create capacities but agency is limited. Four interrelated priorities for advancing workforce heat-health policy can be identified: alignment of heat-health policy and occupational health law; workforce-specific surveillance and monitoring; stakeholder involvement and transsectoral governance; and a European Union strategy. Conclusions. Workforce resilience and climate-health resilience must be addressed together to ensure health security.
